messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Priya Iyer is a 46-year-old non-binary South Asian software engineer who presents with a PCL-5 score of 54, seeking help approximately fourteen months after an incident of police violence that they describe, haltingly and incompletely, as the worst thing that has ever happened to them. Priya is married and works remotely for a mid-sized tech firm, a circumstance that has taken on a significance they did not anticipate when the trauma occurred.

The incident happened on a Saturday afternoon in early autumn. Priya had been cycling home from a farmers' market — a routine they had enjoyed for years — when they were stopped by officers who, within minutes, escalated the encounter into something violent. What Priya can reconstruct of that afternoon is fragmentary: the sound of a radio crackling, the sensation of pavement, the particular quality of afternoon light on the street. They cannot tell the story as a sequence with a beginning, middle, and end, even to themselves. Instead, what surfaces are emotional surges — a wave of terror and humiliation arriving without any accompanying image, as though the feeling has been severed from the event that produced it. When Priya tries to press further into the memory, something intervenes before the recall can complete itself, and they find themselves suddenly thinking about something else entirely, the thread broken. This fractured quality of the memory means that Priya has never been able to fully process what happened, and it feeds directly into a vigilance that now structures their entire day: because the memory offers no coherent narrative, no clear account of what signs preceded the danger, Priya has come to believe that harm can arrive from any direction, without warning, and from anyone at all.

That belief — that you can never know who will harm you — sits at the center of Priya's current experience and radiates outward into nearly everything. The world Priya once understood, one in which institutions were broadly trustworthy and strangers were neutral, has been completely destroyed. And it is precisely this conviction — that the world is fundamentally unreadable and threatening — that keeps pulling Priya back into the memory itself, as though the mind is searching the fragmented record of that afternoon for the warning sign they must have missed, the moment that would explain how ordinary became catastrophic. The belief that danger is everywhere and sourceless makes the memory feel urgently relevant rather than past, and so it surfaces again and again, not as narrative but as sensation, insisting on its own unfinished business. They describe this not as a philosophical shift but as a physical fact, something they feel in their body when they walk into a room. And because Priya now holds the world to be fundamentally unpredictable and threatening, ordinary life has become a landscape of potential cues. Once Priya had settled into that appraisal — that threat could come from any direction, encoded in any interaction — the range of what could function as a trigger expanded accordingly. Things that would once have passed unnoticed now snagged: a delivery driver lingering near the front door, a colleague's voice rising slightly on a call, the particular angle of afternoon light through the home office window. The belief did not merely accompany the triggers; it manufactured them, turning the texture of ordinary life into a continuous stream of potential warnings. People cycling past the window of their home office stop Priya mid-sentence during a code review; the sight of someone on a bicycle triggers an immediate physical reaction — heart rate spiking, hands going cold — and pulls fragments of that afternoon back toward the surface, never quite resolving into a full memory but insistent enough to derail the present moment entirely. Each of these encounters does more than interrupt the present: it arrives with a verdict. When the cyclist passes and the fear floods in, Priya finds themselves thinking, with a clarity that feels irrefutable, that this is simply how the world is now — that anyone could become a threat, that no situation is ever truly readable. The triggers do not merely recall the past; they continuously re-author Priya's understanding of the present, refreshing the conviction that harm is always imminent and always unannounced. Confrontations of any kind, even a mildly tense Slack exchange with a colleague about a deployment timeline, carry the same charge. Priya's body responds as though the danger is current and physical, and in that state the memory presses in again: not images, but the feeling of it, the specific texture of that terror. Living at that sustained pitch of perceived danger, Priya found that the felt sense of threat became its own form of evidence. Feeling this afraid, all the time and in ordinary circumstances, quietly confirmed the thought they worked hardest to resist: that they were not the kind of person who got to feel safe anymore, that the incident had revealed something true about their place in the world rather than something exceptional about that one afternoon.

What Priya finds most difficult to explain, and most shameful, is that even moments of happiness have become triggers. A relaxed Saturday morning, a feeling of ease shared with their spouse over coffee, produces an almost immediate reversal — as though contentment is a signal that something terrible is about to happen. This is consistent with the appraisal that now governs Priya's inner life: that safety is illusory, that happiness is a form of exposure. They have come to feel, with a certainty that embarrasses them, that other people can see what happened to them simply by looking — that the event is somehow written on their face or body. This belief keeps them hypervigilant in any shared space. At the office's quarterly in-person meetings, Priya arrives early to select a seat with their back to the wall and a clear sightline to the exit, and they spend much of those gatherings watching colleagues for signs of threat rather than attending to the agenda.

The hypervigilance, the avoidance of cycling routes and any media depicting police, and the growing difficulty concentrating at work have quietly accumulated into a life that has contracted significantly. Already running at that level of perceived threat, Priya found that the threshold for what registered as a warning signal dropped steadily lower — the background hum of danger they carried into every room made ordinary cues feel like messages their body was compelled to read. A colleague's unexpected knock on the video call, a news alert on their phone, the sound of a siren two streets away: each one landed with a weight it would never have carried before, because Priya's nervous system was already certain that something was coming. Priya's spouse has noticed the withdrawal. It was their spouse who finally said, gently, that something needed to change — and it was that conversation, and the fear that they were losing the last space that felt safe, that brought Priya to seek help. What they most hope for is to be able to tell the story of what happened, in order, from beginning to end. What they are most afraid of is what they might find if they do.
